Tuesday, 8 July 2036. Leo has his final exam, the oral part: the specialist interview with two examiners. One of them is Frau Engel, an engineer at the BVG.
Herr Brandt, you're driving on the M1. Suddenly the front door won't close. What do you do?
First I stop at the next stop. You're not allowed to continue with the door open.
Then the control centre has to be informed. I try to close the door manually. If it can't be closed, it gets locked out of use, and the passengers are asked to use the other doors.
Good. Next question: a signal is hard to see in heavy rain. Which rule applies?
A signal that can't be recognised must be treated as a stop signal. So I stop and drive on sight.
Very good. And what is your most important task as a tram driver?
According to the regulations: what matters is that passenger safety is guaranteed. In my own words: that everyone arrives safe and sound. Including the people who aren't on the tram.
You're thinking of the boy on Schönhauser Allee.
That can't be examined, Herr Brandt. But it's the right answer.
“auf Sicht fahren” = to drive on sight (at a speed that lets you stop within what you can see)
Regulations and technical manuals love “sein + zu”: it's short and impersonal.
The context decides. In regulations it's usually an obligation. In descriptions it's often a possibility.

Leo had already taken the written final exam in June, in a big, cold room at the BVG training centre in Lichtenberg, together with twenty-three other apprentices, among them Abena. For three hours they had answered questions, in a language Leo by now had a better command of than his school German: “Name the measures to be taken immediately in the event of an overhead line failure.” “Explain under what conditions a set of points must be switched manually.” “Describe how the pantograph can be lowered in the event of a fault.” Leo had written until his hand hurt. He had passed, with ninety-one points out of a hundred. Abena with ninety-four. She had told him so, as he told Ludwig, “very diplomatically, but clearly”.

Now two parts were still missing: the oral specialist interview on Tuesday, the eighth of July, and the practical driving exam, scheduled for the end of August, after the wedding in Sibiu. The specialist interview frightened Leo more than anything. He wasn't a man of many words. He was, as his mother said, “a Brandt of the quiet sort”, more like his grandfather when he was young than like his grandfather today. In writing he could explain anything. But when someone looked at him and asked a question, then, as he described it to Abena, “the words in my head suddenly can't be found. As if someone had switched off the overhead line.”

So he practised. He practised with Abena in the canteen, with Kurt Wolff at the depot and, most of all, with Ludwig in the kitchen. Ludwig hadn't driven a tram for twenty-five years, it was true, and the technology had become something else entirely, with screens instead of levers and computers instead of relays. But the questions, Ludwig said, had stayed the same. “What do you do when the door won't close? What do you do when a signal can't be seen? What do you do when a passenger falls over in the carriage?” He asked the questions and Leo answered, haltingly at first, then more fluently, and Ludwig didn't correct the technical side, only what he called “the bearing”. “You talk like someone apologising,” he said. “Talk like someone who drives a tram.”

Hotte had different advice. He came on the Thursday before the exam, listened for half an hour as Ludwig quizzed Leo and then shook his head. “You're doin' it wrong,” he said. “Examiners are people too. They sit there all day and hear the same answer twenty times. They don't wanna hear what's in the book. They know that already. They wanna hear if you know why it's in the book.” He leaned forward. “In nineteen sixty-eight I sat in on exams too, as a young instructor. Know who I failed? The one who knew everything by heart and never asked why. And know who I let through? This Ludwig here. On the question about braking distance he said: no idea how many metres exactly. But I know I'd rather brake too early than too late.” Ludwig protested that he had known the exact figure back then and had only forgotten it out of nerves. Hotte waved this away.

One evening, three days before the exam, Ludwig took something out of the cupboard in the hall that Leo had never seen: a small, worn notebook with a grey cover and the inscription “Dienstvorschrift für den Straßenbahnfahrdienst, VEB Kombinat Berliner Verkehrsbetriebe, 1966” (Service regulations for tram drivers). It was the rulebook Ludwig had learnt from, and it was full of pencil notes, underlinings and, on the last page, a drawing showing a tram with a smiling face in its windscreen. “Ingrid drew that,” said Ludwig. “The evening before my exam. She said I should look at it when I didn't know what to do any more.” Leo looked at the drawing for a long time. It looked exactly like the drawing little Jonas had given him in March.

Leo leafed through the old notebook. The language was even stiffer than today, even more nouns, even more “ist zu”. “When approaching a stop, the speed is to be calculated in such a way that stopping at the designated place is ensured at all times.” “The audible warning signal is to be operated immediately in the event of danger.” “The driver is to behave towards passengers at all times in a polite and helpful manner.” Next to this last sentence someone had written something in pencil in the margin, in small, neat handwriting that wasn't Ludwig's: “And friendly. That isn't in there, but it's the most important thing. I.” Leo read it twice. Then he looked at his grandfather. “Can I take the notebook with me on Tuesday?” he asked. “Not to copy from. Just in my pocket.”

Ludwig gave it to him without hesitating. On Tuesday morning, at half past six, Lena was standing at his door with a lunch box containing two cheese rolls, an apple and a slice of cake, “for the nerves”. In the box Elif had put a note which, in her round, neat handwriting, said only: “Don't forget the bridge. First think, then connect, then speak.” Leo didn't understand the note straight away. Only on the S-Bahn did he remember what Elif had done with the proofs, with her little bridges drawn between sentences that had no connection. He laughed, alone in the carriage, and an elderly lady looked at him suspiciously. Then he resolved not to say a single sentence in the exam without a bridge: first, then, after that, that's why, still. It was, he thought, like laying tracks. Without tracks, no tram can run.

On Tuesday at nine, Leo sat in a small meeting room at the training centre in front of two examiners: an older man with glasses called Herr Brenner, who, as Leo found out later, had done his training thirty years ago together with Kurt Wolff, and a woman of about fifty with short grey hair and a very direct gaze, Frau Engel, a qualified engineer, head of the vehicle engineering department. Frau Engel asked the questions. She asked them quickly, precisely, without a smile. What do you do when the door can't be closed? What rule applies to a signal that can't be recognised? How can the pantograph be lowered in the event of an overhead line fault, and in what order are the measures to be taken?

Leo answered. At first he answered quietly, looking down, like someone apologising. Then, at the third question, he felt the small grey notebook in his jacket pocket and thought of the drawing on the last page and the sentence in the margin. And he raised his head. He looked at Frau Engel, directly, and explained, in calm, clear sentences, step by step, how the pantograph can be lowered, which switches have to be operated and in what order, when the control centre has to be informed and when the passengers. He spoke, as Ludwig said later when Leo told him about it, “like someone who drives a tram”. Herr Brenner nodded several times. Frau Engel noted something on her sheet.

Then came the last question, which wasn't on any exam sheet. Frau Engel put down her pen, leaned back and looked at Leo, for the first time without severity. “Herr Brandt,” she said, “what, in your opinion, is your most important task as a tram driver?” Leo didn't hesitate. “According to the regulations,” he said, “what matters is that passenger safety is guaranteed.” He paused. “In my own words: that everyone arrives safe and sound. Including the people who aren't on the tram. And,” he added, after a moment, touching, without realising it, the jacket pocket with the notebook, “you have to be friendly. That isn't in the regulations. But it's the most important thing.”

Frau Engel looked at him for a long time. Then she said something Leo wasn't expecting. “You're the driver from Schönhauser Allee. Zero point seven seconds.” Leo nodded. “I've seen the recording,” said Frau Engel. “We show it in training now. As an example.” She was silent for a moment. “My son is called Jonas too,” she then said quietly. “He's nine.” And then, back in her matter-of-fact tone, as if she hadn't said anything personal: “Your answer can't be examined, Herr Brandt. But it's the right one.” Herr Brenner cleared his throat and said that the exam was over, that he would be told the result in a quarter of an hour, and would he please wait outside.

The quarter of an hour was the longest of Leo's life, longer than the zero point seven seconds on Schönhauser Allee, which, as he later confessed to Abena, had afterwards felt like an hour. He sat on a hard chair in the corridor, under a poster with the words “Sicherheit geht vor” (Safety first), and turned the small grey notebook over in his hands. Then the door opened. Herr Brenner came out, shook his hand and said only: “Very good. One point three. Congratulations. Now there's just the drive in August and then you're one of us.” Behind him, in the doorway, stood Frau Engel. She didn't smile. But she nodded, once, the way Grete had nodded when she found Elif in the hall. And Leo understood that for some people that is the same thing.

Three people were waiting for him outside the training centre. Abena, who had swapped a shift specially. Thomas, his father, in a suit, straight from the office in Adlershof, with a face that couldn't decide whether to be proud or nervous. And, on a bench in the sun, with his stick between his knees and his old tram driver's cap on his head, Ludwig, who had come by S-Bahn, alone, for the first time in two years, against Lena's express advice. Leo went over to him, sat down beside him and gave him back the small grey notebook. “One point three,” he said. Ludwig took the notebook, opened it at the last page, with the drawing and the sentence in the margin, and looked at it for a long time. “She would have said: see?” he said at last. “She always said that when she was right. Which was almost always.” Then he handed the notebook back to Leo. “Keep it,” he said. “You still need it. In August.”

In the evening the brass bell rang in the café «Bei Ingrid», although it was after four o'clock and the felt had long been lifted. Once when Leo came in. Then a second time when Abena came in, who had also passed, with one point zero, which this time she announced not diplomatically but very loudly. Then a third time, without anyone coming in, because it was Dr Vogt, who had the day off and was already sitting at the table by the window and stood up to ring it with his finger, very softly, as his own rule required. “For the passengers,” he said, “who will arrive safe and sound. Every day. Without ever knowing it.” Leo blushed. Lena brought cake. And Hotte, who of course was there too, even though it was a Tuesday, raised his glass and said only: “One of us.” It was the shortest praise Leo had ever received. And the most beautiful.
